subject: Computer Science
topic: Tracing algorithms, loop invariants and edge cases
scope: Language-independent algorithm reasoning. Syntax-specific examination conventions and complete programming-course coverage are not claimed.
prerequisites: Read a list indexed from zero.
objectives: Trace state changes in a loop.
Use an invariant to justify a simple algorithm.

notes.heading: State and order of execution
paragraphs: An algorithm is a finite description of steps intended to solve a class of problems. To trace it, record the current values of relevant variables after each executed statement, not merely after each line as printed. Assignment replaces a stored value; it is not an equation asserting equality forever. In x=x+1, the old value is read before the new value is stored. A condition determines which branch executes, and a loop condition determines whether another iteration begins. Write down initial state, index convention and expected input constraints before tracing, because an off-by-one error often begins with an unstated boundary assumption.

notes.heading: An invariant explains why a loop works
paragraphs: A loop invariant is a statement about the program state that holds at a specified point in every iteration. For a running sum, an invariant at the start of iteration i is that total equals the sum of the first i elements. Initially i=0 and total=0, so it holds for the empty prefix. Adding element i and incrementing i preserves the statement for the longer prefix. At termination i equals the list length, so total is the required complete sum. This argument has three parts: initialisation, preservation and connection to the final result. A true invariant that says nothing useful about the output is not enough by itself.

notes.heading: Boundaries, termination and efficiency
paragraphs: Test ordinary inputs and edge cases: an empty list, one element, repeated values, negative values and values at stated bounds. Tests can reveal defects, but a finite collection of passing tests does not prove correctness for every permitted input. Termination requires separate reasoning; for an index increasing by one toward a finite list length, the number of unprocessed elements decreases until it reaches zero. Efficiency describes how resources grow with input size. A single pass through n elements is linear time under a constant-cost-per-element model. Do not confuse the number of source-code lines with running time, since a short nested loop can execute many operations.

notes.heading: Correctness, termination and resource use
paragraphs: A loop invariant is a statement that is true before an iteration and is preserved by each completed iteration. To use it as an argument, explain initialisation, maintenance and what it implies at termination. For a running total, an invariant might state that the accumulator equals the sum of exactly the elements already processed. Saying the loop works because it adds numbers is weaker: it does not specify which elements have been included or whether any were skipped or counted twice.

Correct output on selected tests does not by itself prove correctness for every valid input. Tests should include boundary cases, duplicates, negative values where permitted, and inputs that challenge each branch. A termination argument needs a measure that progresses toward a bound, not merely the presence of a loop condition. Correctness and efficiency are separate questions: two algorithms can produce identical answers while using different amounts of time or memory. State the input-size variable before discussing growth, and distinguish a count of operations from elapsed time on a particular machine. Preconditions such as a nonempty list or sorted data must be checked or explicitly documented.

notes.heading: Proving a running maximum
paragraphs: For a nonempty list, initialise a running maximum from the first element, not from a convenient constant such as zero. Before each subsequent iteration, the stored value should equal the maximum of exactly the elements already processed. Comparing the next element and retaining the larger value preserves that invariant. At termination every element has been processed, so the invariant yields the required result. This argument also explains an all-negative test: a zero initial value introduces a candidate that was never in the input. The empty-list case needs an explicit contract, such as returning no result or reporting invalid input. A trace demonstrates one run; an invariant explains all runs satisfying the preconditions.

workedExamples.prompt: Trace total=0; for each value in [3,-1,4], set total=total+value.
steps: After 4, total is 6; each prefix sum matches the processed elements.

workedExamples.prompt: A maximum-finding algorithm starts max=0 and scans [-5,-2,-9]. Identify the defect and repair.
steps: No negative input is greater than zero, so the algorithm incorrectly returns zero.
For a nonempty list initialise max to its first element, then scan the rest.
Specify a separate policy for empty input instead of assuming a maximum exists.
workedExamples.answer: Initialise from a real element for nonempty input; explicitly handle the empty case.

workedExamples.prompt: Give an invariant for summing a list from left to right with total initially zero.
steps: Before processing any entries, total=0 equals the sum of the empty processed prefix.
After adding the next entry, total equals the sum of the enlarged prefix.
At termination the prefix is the entire list, so total is the required sum.
workedExamples.answer: Before each iteration, total equals the sum of the entries processed so far.

workedExamples.prompt: Trace a running maximum over [-8, -3, -11, -4], initialised from the first element. Give the stored value after each remaining element and the final result.
steps: Neither -11 nor -4 exceeds -3, so the value stays -3.
All four elements have been processed; -3 is a member of the input and is at least every element.

misconceptions.claim: Passing three examples proves an algorithm correct.
misconceptions.correction: Examples test selected cases; correctness over a domain needs broader reasoning or proof.

misconceptions.claim: A loop invariant changes to a different claim every iteration.
misconceptions.correction: The same relationship holds at the stated point, although variable values change.

questions.prompt: Trace x=2 followed by x=x+3 and then x=2*x. What is final x?
solution: The first assignment gives x=5.
The second uses that updated value and gives x=10.
markingPoints: Use the updated intermediate value 5.
Obtain 10.

questions.prompt: Which input most directly exposes the flaw in initialising a nonempty-list maximum to zero?
options: A list containing only positive numbers
A list containing zero and a positive number
A list containing one positive number
A list containing only negative numbers
questions.answer: A list containing only negative numbers
solution: Zero is not necessarily a member of the input.
If all values are negative, none replaces the incorrect initial maximum.
markingPoints: Select an all-negative list.

questions.prompt: Give an invariant for a loop counting positive values in the first i elements of a list.
questions.answer: At the start of iteration i, count equals the number of values greater than zero among indices 0 through i-1.
solution: Specify the exact point at which the invariant holds.
Relate the counter to the processed prefix, excluding unprocessed elements.
markingPoints: Identify the processed prefix precisely.
State that count matches positive values in that prefix.

questions.prompt: Explain correctness and termination of summing a finite list by adding one element per iteration, starting with total=0.
questions.answer: Initially total is the empty-prefix sum. Each iteration adds exactly the next element, preserving the prefix-sum invariant. The unprocessed element count decreases by one until zero, at which point total equals the complete sum.
solution: Establish the invariant initially.
Explain its preservation by one iteration.
Use a decreasing unprocessed count for termination and connect the final invariant to the answer.
markingPoints: Justify initialisation.
Justify preservation.
Justify termination and the final result.

questions.prompt: A binary search implementation is tested on one sorted list and then used on arbitrary unsorted lists. Explain the missing precondition and why passing that test is insufficient.
questions.answer: Binary search relies on ordering to discard a region safely. An unsorted list can contain the target in a discarded region. One successful test on a valid sorted input does not establish correctness when the precondition is violated.
solution: Identify sorted input as the relevant precondition.
Explain how ordering supports discarding part of the search space.
Separate one successful test from a guarantee for other inputs.
markingPoints: Identify sorted input as the relevant precondition.
Explain how ordering supports discarding part of the search space.
Separate one successful test from a guarantee for other inputs.

questions.prompt: Trace a running maximum over [-8, -3, -11, -4], initialised from the first element. Give the stored value after each remaining element and the final result.
questions.answer: Stored values: -3, -3, -3. The maximum is -3.
solution: After comparing -3 with -8, retain -3.
Neither -11 nor -4 exceeds -3, so the value stays -3.
All four elements have been processed; -3 is a member of the input and is at least every element.
markingPoints: After comparing -3 with -8, retain -3.
Neither -11 nor -4 exceeds -3, so the value stays -3.

questions.prompt: A maximum-finding loop starts with best = 0. Explain its failure on [-8, -3] and give a repair including the empty-list case.
questions.answer: It returns 0, which is absent from the input. Initialise from the first element for a nonempty list and handle an empty list explicitly.
solution: Neither negative input exceeds the incorrect initial value 0.
Initialising from the first input establishes the running-maximum invariant.
Define and handle the empty-list result before accessing the first element.
markingPoints: Neither negative input exceeds the incorrect initial value 0.
Initialising from the first input establishes the running-maximum invariant.
Define and handle the empty-list result before accessing the first element.
